differential: Bacterial meningitis
High-grade fever, severe headache, vomiting, and altered mental status (lethargy/confusion) are classic signs of meningitis in a child.
Viral meningitis
Presents similarly to bacterial meningitis with fever, headache, vomiting, and altered mental status, though typically less severe.
Encephalitis
Fever with prominent altered mental status (lethargy and confusion) suggests brain parenchymal inflammation beyond meningeal involvement.
Brain abscess
Can present with fever, headache, vomiting, and altered mental status due to localized intracranial infection with mass effect.
Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM)
Post-infectious immune-mediated CNS inflammation can cause fever, headache, and encephalopathy in children.
eliminated: None
Insufficient information at this stage to rule out any diagnoses definitively.

differential: Meningococcal meningitis

Pneumococcal meningitis
Bacterial meningitis with purulent nasal discharge (suggesting sinusitis source), fever, neck rigidity, and altered mental status in a young child.
Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis
Bacterial meningitis presenting with classic triad of fever, neck rigidity, and altered mental status, though less common if vaccinated.

Petechial rash starting on extremities, high fever, headache, and altered mental status could represent rickettsial infection with meningeal involvement.
Acute bacterial sinusitis with intracranial extension
Purulent nasal discharge with severe headache, fever, and meningeal signs suggests complicated sinusitis with epidural abscess or meningitis.
eliminated: Viral meningitis
The presence of petechiae, hypotension, and severity of presentation make bacterial etiology much more likely than viral.

differential: Meningococcal meningitis

eliminated: Viral meningitis

differential: Terminal complement deficiency (C5-C9)
Confirmed by CH50 = 0 and recurrent Neisseria meningitidis infection, which characteristically affects patients with membrane attack complex deficiencies.
Meningococcal meningitis with septicemia
Confirmed by CSF culture positive for Neisseria meningitidis with associated hypotension, petechiae, and meningeal signs indicating systemic meningococcal disease.
Properdin deficiency
X-linked complement deficiency predisposing specifically to severe and recurrent Neisseria meningitidis infections with high mortality.
C3 deficiency
Rare complement deficiency that can present with absent CH50 and increased susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria including meningococcus.
Factor H or Factor I deficiency
Alternative pathway dysregulation causing secondary complement consumption with increased susceptibility to Neisseria infections and low CH50.

Asplenia/hyposplenism

C3 deficiency
